title: The Royal Game of Ur
why: A 4,500-year-old game whose rules were recovered from a clay tablet in the British Museum.

title: Go
why: Simple rules that are older than chess, with more possible games than atoms in the universe.

title: The Evolution of Trust
why: A playable explainer on game theory and why people cooperate or cheat.

title: Hex
why: A game that cannot end in a draw. It was invented twice, once by John Nash.

title: Interactive fiction
why: Text adventures never went away. Thousands of free story games can be played in a browser.

title: Mancala
why: A family of seed-sowing games played across Africa and Asia, on boards or in holes in the ground.

title: Senet
why: A game from ancient Egypt, found in Tutankhamun's tomb. The original rules are lost.

title: Hnefatafl
why: The Viking board game where the two sides are unequal: a king tries to escape a larger army.

title: Nim
why: A game with piles of matchsticks that mathematics has solved completely. Learn the trick and you cannot lose.
how: Short read, then try it on someone

title: Shogi
why: Japanese chess, where the pieces you capture change sides and come back as your own.

title: The Landlord's Game
why: The 1904 game that Monopoly grew from, designed to show why monopolies are bad.

title: Kriegsspiel
why: The 19th-century Prussian army wargame that is the ancestor of modern hobby wargames.

title: Nomic
why: A game in which changing the rules is a move. It was invented by a philosopher.

title: Gamebooks
why: Books where you choose what happens next and turn to that page. Some need dice and a pencil.

title: Chess puzzles
why: Lichess serves an endless stream of free puzzles taken from real games.

title: Pyramid games
why: One set of stackable plastic pyramids and hundreds of different games invented for it.

title: The maths of Dobble
why: Any two cards share exactly one symbol. The trick comes from geometry.

title: Sprouts
why: A pencil-and-paper game invented by two mathematicians. A few dots are enough to start.
how: Read, then play on a napkin

title: AlphaGo and move 37
why: In 2016 a program played a Go move that no professional would have chosen, and it won the game.

title: Intransitive dice
why: Three dice where A usually beats B, B usually beats C, and C usually beats A.
